lines.text: Coastal kingdoms, a French colony on a great river, a Marxist state and an oil nation. This is the story of the Republic of the Congo.
On the Atlantic coast, the Kingdom of Loango traded with Europeans for centuries, in ivory and, tragically, in people.
Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza, born in 1852, would explore the river and claim its north bank for France.
In 1880 a French post was set up on the river, facing what is now Kinshasa. It took the name Brazzaville.
Fulbert Youlou, born in 1917, would become a priest, and later the country's first president.
In 1935 Odzala was set aside as a park, one of Africa's oldest, home to forest elephants and gorillas.
Denis Sassou Nguesso, born in 1943, would one day hold power for more than four decades.
In 1940 Brazzaville became the capital of Free France, and in 1944 de Gaulle's government met there to promise reform in Africa.
In 1960 the Republic of the Congo became independent from France, on the north bank of the river.
In 1969 it became a Marxist people's republic, and it stayed one until 1992.
In 1997 civil war broke out. It ended two years later with Sassou Nguesso back in power, where he has stayed.
From Loango to the oil fields, Congo's river still carries its long story.
